learning_outcomes.text: Understanding and mastery of fundamental concepts regarding the general laws of Physics (Kinematics, Dynamics, Thermodynamics) and their application to solving engineering problems.
Ability to pose and solve problems in physics and engineering.
Teamwork.
Ability to perform laboratory setups and practical experiments.
Ability to perform and interpret calculations from experiments performed.
Effective and appropriate use of information resources.
Autonomous learning.
Completion of a practical activity and corresponding report writing in English.
Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, which enables them to learn new methods and theories, and provides them with versatility to adapt to new situations.

Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning and to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills and abilities in the field of Mechanical Industrial Engineering.
Ability to work in a multilingual and multidisciplinary environment.
Understanding and mastery of basic concepts about the general laws of mechanics, thermodynamics, fields and waves and electromagnetism and their application for solving engineering problems.
Basic knowledge about the use and programming of computers, operating systems, databases and computer programs with application in engineering.
Capacity for analysis and synthesis.
Capacity for organization and time planning.
Capacity for oral expression.
Capacity for written expression.
Ability to learn and work autonomously.
Problem-solving ability.
Critical reasoning/logical analysis ability.
Ability to apply knowledge to practice.
Ability to work effectively in a team.

Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is typically at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes aspects that imply knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students are able to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competencies typically demonstrated by elaborating and defending arguments and solving problems within their field of study.
Students have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific or ethical issues.
Students can transmit information, ideas, problems and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Students have developed the learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

syllabus_topics: KINEMATIC MAGNITUDES (position, velocity, acceleration) AND EQUATIONS OF MOTION
UNIFORMLY ACCELERATED RECTILINEAR MOTION (UARM): Parabolic motion, free fall
CONTACT FORCE: normal reaction and friction
EQUATIONS OF MOTION IN NON-INERTIAL SYSTEMS: fictitious forces
ANGULAR MOMENTUM OF A RIGID BODY
AIR TRACK (UNIFORM RECTILINEAR MOTION AND UNIFORMLY ACCELERATED RECTILINEAR MOTION, AND NEWTON'S 2ND LAW)
MEASUREMENT OF THE RESTORING CONSTANT OF A SPRING (HOOKE'S LAW)
MECHANICAL ENERGY VARIATION. KINETIC AND POTENTIAL ENERGY
MOMENT OF INERTIA IN A RIGID BODY
teaching_methods: Learning with significant emphasis on laboratory practices
Completion of theoretical-practical exercises in the classroom using a Problem Collection
Group laboratory practices and report writing
assessment_rules: The final grade is a weighted sum: Laboratory Practices (20%), Partial Exam 1 (40%), Partial Exam 2 (40%). To be evaluated, attendance at Laboratory Practices is mandatory. If this condition is not met, the final grade will be 4.5 (fail) even if the total score exceeds 5.0. Continuous assessment is maintained for the second examination call. Students who passed the laboratory practices in a previous academic year may retain their grade, but have the right to retake them. For a single evaluation, the grading consists of a practical exam (20%) and a theoretical and problem-solving exam (80%).
